strengths: Interesting and useful negative finding: the paper systematically demonstrates that discussion-based orchestration methods (MoA, LLM-Debate, MAV) that help frontier LLMs actually degrade SLM performance (up to 5.5% drops), challenging the assumption that orchestration transfers across model scales; the failure attribution analysis (groupthink classification in Appendix C) adds supporting evidence.

The proposed method is simple, training-free, and well-motivated: per-model self-consistency as a confidence signal with validation-accuracy tie-breaking is a sensible design given SLMs' weak deliberation abilities.
Evaluation covers multiple benchmarks (MATH, GPQA, GSM8K) and several baselines, including self-consistency and Agent Forest, with standard errors reported over multiple runs.

The compute scaling analysis (number of models vs. samples per model) and the model selection search (union accuracy with contradiction penalty) are practically useful, and the observation that union accuracy rises while actual accuracy plateaus or declines is a valuable insight.
The demonstration that a two-SLM ensemble can match or beat Qwen-2.5 72B on GPQA and GSM8K is an attention-grabbing and practically relevant result.
weaknesses: Limited novelty of the core method: SLM-MUX is essentially per-model self-consistency followed by argmax over confidence scores with a validation-accuracy tie-break. Both ingredients are well-known (self-consistency, confidence-based selection, model routing), and the paper itself cites closely related work (e.g., confidence-improved self-consistency, Agent Forest). The contribution is more an empirical study than a new technique.

Baseline fairness is questionable: discussion-based baselines use original prompts designed for frontier models, while SLM-MUX gets a bespoke design; more importantly, in Table 1 Single-Best-SC actually outperforms SLM-MUX on GPQA (42.4 vs. 42.1), which undercuts the headline claim of consistent superiority over existing approaches.

Compute parity is not carefully controlled: SLM-MUX uses k samples per model per query (and 'best' scaling up to 9), while comparisons to Qwen-2.5 72B and Single-Best are not token-matched. Figure 1 suggests token usage is considered, but the accuracy-vs-compute accounting across Table 1/Table 4 comparisons is inconsistent.

The theoretical analysis is elementary: a binomial majority-vote calculation showing A(N,p) > p only when p > 0.5, plus the observation that selecting the max-p model approximates A(N, pmax). This is intuitive but does not constitute a substantive theoretical contribution; assumptions (independence, fixed per-question p) are not discussed.

The model selection search requires exhaustive search over model subsets with multiple generations per model per question on a 500-question validation set, which is costly and not scalable (acknowledged as a limitation), and the λ=1 hyperparameter choice is not ablated.

The groupthink failure analysis depends on LLM-based labeling (an analyzer LLM plus a labeling LLM), whose reliability is not validated against human judgment, weakening the central mechanistic claim.

The method's confidence measure fails when models are consistently but confidently wrong (the contradiction-penalty partially addresses this only during model selection, not at inference), and the framework is static and question-agnostic, limiting applicability.

Some experimental details are thin or inconsistent: e.g., the relationship between the naive 3-model setup in Section 4.2 and the searched 2-model setups in Section 4.3/4.4 makes the aggregate picture hard to interpret, and discussion of which results hold across which model groups is scattered.

strengths: Timely and clearly motivated problem: studying whether LLM orchestration methods transfer to small language models, with a useful negative finding that discussion-based methods (MoA, Debate, MAV) can degrade SLM performance, supported by a groupthink failure analysis in the appendix.
Reasonably broad empirical coverage: three benchmarks (MATH, GPQA, GSM8K), multiple orchestration baselines, and ablations over number of models and samples per model.
The proposed method is simple, training-free, and easy to implement; the model-selection search with a union-accuracy/contradiction-penalty objective is a sensible, well-motivated heuristic.
The paper is generally well organized and readable, with ablations (Figures 7-9) that transparently show where the method does and does not help.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The core method reduces to: sample k answers per model, take each model's majority answer, and pick the answer of the model whose majority answer is most self-consistent (ties broken by validation accuracy). Confidence/consistency-based selection is well explored (e.g., self-consistency, Taubenfeld et al. 2025 on confidence improving self-consistency, FrugalGPT-style selection, RouterDC, Agent Forest). The model-selection step is an exhaustive search over 5 models with a hand-tuned objective, which is not a substantive algorithmic contribution.

Baseline fairness and compute matching are unclear and arguably unfavorable. SLM-MUX consumes multiple samples per model (3-9), while Single-Best is greedy and the SC baseline configuration is underspecified. On GPQA in Table 1, Single-Best-SC (42.4) actually matches/beats SLM-MUX (42.1), yet the headline claims of gains of 'up to 8.8% on GPQA' are asserted. In the compute-scaled setting (Table 3, 'Samples=best'), the margin over Agent Forest shrinks to +0.3/+1.2/+2.2, which undercuts the significance of the architectural contribution.

Claims are stronger than the evidence. The comparison against Qwen 2.5 72B ignores total inference compute: an ensemble of 2 models x many samples can consume comparable or more tokens than the 72B model; no cost- or token-matched comparison against the large model is provided, despite token usage being reported elsewhere (Figure 1, Table 7).

The 'fundamental limitation' claim about discussion-based orchestration on SLMs rests on three methods, two to three benchmarks, and essentially one model composition, without controlling for prompt sensitivity or aggregation protocols; prior work (e.g., Du et al. themselves, and self-correction literature) already suggested debate/self-correction needs sufficiently capable models, so the finding is less surprising than presented.

The theoretical analysis is shallow. The binomial argument assumes a fixed per-question success probability p and independent samples, and ignores the selection bias introduced by choosing p_max across models; the 'Type 1/2/3' taxonomy is informal and yields no predictive or prescriptive insight beyond 'consistency helps when p > 0.5'.

Notation and method description are inconsistent: the objective is written as O(S) = Acc(S) - lambda*Contradiction(S) while the defined quantity is UnionAcc(S); Acc(S) is never formally defined; temperature and sample counts differ across sections (0.3 with 3 rounds in Sec 4.2 vs 0.5 with 3 repeats in Sec 4.3); the project page URL in the abstract is blank, hurting reproducibility.

Sensitivity to key design choices is not analyzed: the hyperparameter lambda is fixed at 1 without ablation, the validation set is only 500 questions, and the tie-breaking rule using global validation accuracy is coarse (as the paper's own Figure 12 example illustrates, ties between a confident-wrong and confident-right model are resolved by a nearly uninformative historical accuracy).

Static, question-agnostic design: the paper acknowledges the ensemble is fixed per benchmark via costly exhaustive search, which limits practical applicability and contrasts with adaptive routing baselines that are cited but not compared against (e.g., RouteLLM, FrugalGPT).

strengths: The paper identifies a valuable and counterintuitive negative result: discussion-based orchestration methods (MoA, LLM-Debate, MAV) that help frontier LLMs actually hurt SLM performance, with a systematic comparison across model scales, methods, and benchmarks (Figure 5), plus a reasonably careful failure analysis (Appendix C, Table 5).

The proposed SLM-MUX is simple, training-free, and practical; it avoids error amplification by selecting the most self-consistent model's output, and gains are consistent and substantial across MATH, GPQA, and GSM8K (Table 1) versus strong baselines including the best single model with self-consistency (Single-Best-SC) and Agent Forest (Table 3).

The model selection search with Union Accuracy plus a Contradiction Penalty is a sensible formulation of complementarity, and the paper honestly shows the trade-off as models are added (Figures 7 and 9) rather than claiming uniform scaling gains.

The empirical demonstration that two orchestrated SLMs can match/exceed Qwen-2.5 72B on GPQA and GSM8K (Table 4) is an interesting headline result, and the paper discusses limitations (static selection, self-consistency as confidence proxy) candidly.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: SLM-MUX is essentially per-model self-consistency plus a confidence-based selector with validation-accuracy tie-breaking. The authors themselves cite prior work that consistency correlates with correctness (Wang et al., 2023; Taubenfeld et al., 2025); the architectural contribution is a heuristic aggregation rule rather than a new technique, and the theoretical analysis (binomial threshold argument in Section 5) is elementary.

Compute parity concerns for the headline claims: comparisons against Qwen-2.5 72B (Table 4) and Agent Forest use the 'best' number of samples found by scaling, but total token/compute costs of SLM-MUX versus the single large model are not clearly reported; Figure 1 shows MATH only, and the efficient-system framing needs compute-matched evidence across all benchmarks.

Evaluation details that weaken rigor: the objective is inconsistently written (UnionAcc defined, then O(S) = Acc(S) − λ·Contradiction(S) with Acc(S) never defined); λ=1 is chosen without ablation; how the 'two representative two-model combinations' were chosen from search results for test evaluation is vague, creating cherry-picking risk; the groupthink failure analysis relies on LLM-labeled attributions, which is circular and prone to confirmation bias.

Baselines may be under-tuned: discussion-based methods use original prompts and workflows designed for frontier models; adapting prompts or aggregation for SLMs is not explored, so the claimed architectural-level advantage could partly reflect baseline misconfiguration. Simple pooled/weighted majority voting over all models' samples at matched sample budgets is also missing.

Reproducibility gaps: the project page and code link is empty in the manuscript; validation sets are only 500 questions sampled from training splits with multiple re-sampling rounds, and small sample sizes produce large standard errors on GPQA (±2.3 to ±3.5) that weaken some comparative claims.

strengths: Clear and well-supported negative finding: the paper systematically demonstrates that discussion-based orchestration methods (MoA, LLM-Debate, MAV) that help frontier LLMs actually degrade performance when applied to SLMs, with an instructive groupthink failure analysis (59.5% of failures attributed to groupthink) and a prompt-sensitivity study showing the gap is not a prompt artifact.

The proposed SLM-MUX is simple, training-free, and well-motivated: per-question routing to the most self-consistent model with validation-accuracy tie-breaking is a clean design that sidesteps the error amplification of text-exchange methods.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: three reasoning benchmarks (MATH, GPQA, GSM8K), multiple baseline families (single model, self-consistency, discussion-based, Agent Forest), compute-scaling studies along two axes (number of models, samples per model), test-set validation of scaling trends, and search-set size stability analysis.

Useful model selection formulation: the Union Accuracy vs. Contradiction Penalty objective captures interaction effects between models (overconfident wrong answers suppressing correct ones) that accuracy-only selection criteria miss, with reasonable theoretical framing as upper/lower bounds.

Good breadth of generalization experiments: extension to open-ended generation (HumanEval with embedding-based consistency), frontier LLM pairs (GPT-4o + Gemini-2.5-Flash), and domain-specific fine-tuned models; strong GPQA result (+~10 points over best single model at frontier scale).

Honest limitations section and detailed appendix (failure analysis prompts, single-model accuracies, variance estimation, random-selection ablation showing the architecture itself accounts for gains).
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the core mechanism is essentially self-consistency confidence plus per-question routing/model selection, building directly on known consistency-correctness correlations (Wang et al. 2023; Taubenfeld et al. 2025) and existing routing/selection literature (RouteLLM, FrugalGPT, RouterDC, Archon). The main contribution is empirical rather than methodological.

Comparisons are not compute-matched in Table 1: SLM-MUX samples multiple responses per model at temperature 0.3, while discussion-based baselines run at temperature 0 with single samples. The headline gains (up to 13.4% on MATH) conflate the orchestration architecture with additional sampling compute; only partial controls exist (Single-Best-SC baseline).

Headline claims are somewhat stronger than the evidence: on GPQA, Single-Best-SC (42.4) actually marginally outperforms SLM-MUX (42.1) in Table 1, yet the abstract emphasizes 'up to 8.8% improvement on GPQA' relative to weaker baselines; the paper should foreground the comparison against the strongest baseline rather than the weakest.

The theoretical analysis is thin and rests on unrealistic assumptions: the Hoeffding-bound argument assumes incorrect answers are scattered rather than clustered, which is implausible for multiple-choice benchmarks with few options (wrong answers are by construction concentrated on the distractors), and per-question probabilities p_i are unobservable; the analysis is intuition, not a tight characterization.

The model selection objective introduces a hyperparameter λ set to 1 without sensitivity analysis, and the search relies on an exhaustive enumeration over a small pool (5 models); scalability of the search to realistic model zoos is unaddressed (the authors acknowledge this in limitations, but it bounds practical significance).

Some evaluation details raise questions: validation sets of 500 questions sampled from training splits are used for both selection and scaling decisions, and the marginal gains from the search procedure over random combinations (e.g., +0.1 to +1.7 on GPQA) suggest the selection component contributes modestly relative to the architecture.

Static, dataset-specific model selections reduce practical appeal: the best combination differs per benchmark, and the method requires per-benchmark validation compute, which weakens the 'multi-core alternative to scaling' framing.

strengths: Clear motivation and a useful empirical finding: discussion-based orchestration methods (MoA, LLM-Debate, MAV), which work for frontier LLMs, actually degrade SLM performance; the groupthink failure analysis (Appendix C) and prompt-sensitivity stress test add credibility to this claim.

SLM-MUX is simple, training-free, and practical; the pipeline (independent sampling -> per-model majority answer -> consistency-based selection -> validation-accuracy tie-break) is well specified (Algorithm 1, Figure 3).

Comprehensive evaluation: multiple benchmarks (MATH, GPQA, GSM8K), both SLMs and frontier LLMs, ablations on model selection and compute scaling, generalization to open-ended generation (HumanEval) and domain-specific fine-tuned models, plus useful analyses (search-set stability, random-combination baseline, effective combination rate).

Reasonable theoretical framing: a Hoeffding-style bound for selecting the strongest model by consistency, and a binomial analysis explaining why per-question routing beats pooled voting (Appendix D.2).
Appendices provide prompt templates, variance estimates, and dataset licenses, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The core method reduces to per-model self-consistency followed by confidence-based selection/routing, which is a natural combination of well-known ideas (self-consistency, consistency-correctness correlation already cited as known); the 'architecture' contribution (Figure 2d) is essentially 'no discussion, just select by confidence.'

The headline gains are largely against weak baselines. Compared to Single-Best-SC (the strongest legitimate baseline), the improvements are marginal or non-existent: on GPQA, SLM-MUX scores 42.1 vs 42.4 for Single-Best-SC, i.e., it is actually below the best self-consistency baseline, yet the abstract and Section 4.2 emphasize gains 'up to 8.8%' over discussion-based methods. This selective comparison weakens the central claim.

The claim that two SLMs match/beat Qwen 2.5 72B requires substantial test-time compute (searched model selection plus up to 9 samples per model) and is not accompanied by a rigorous compute-matched comparison against the large model or against Single-Best-SC at equal token budgets.

The model selection objective O(S) = UnionAcc - lambda*Contradiction is heuristic; the connection to actual SLM-MUX accuracy is only argued loosely (upper/lower bound intuition), lambda sensitivity is not studied (only lambda=1 is used), and the search is exhaustive, which the authors themselves acknowledge as slow and costly.

The theoretical analysis rests on a strong and unrealistic assumption (unique correct answer, incorrect answers scattered, per-question model accuracies independent of the question), and treats per-question 'routing to the strongest model' as achievable, which the paper's own contradiction-penalty analysis contradicts.

Some experimental presentation is confusing or inconsistent: temperature and sampling settings differ across sections (0.3 vs 0.5 vs temperature=0 for baselines), Figure 1 token-usage accounting is unclear, and there are editorial issues (e.g., 'GSM' vs GSM8K in the abstract, duplicated text in Section 3.2, missing project-page URL).
Model pool is small (5 SLMs) and results are benchmark-specific (e.g., scaling behavior differs across MATH/GPQA/GSM8K), limiting generality of the scaling conclusions.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem statement: the paper provides a systematic, controlled evaluation showing that discussion-based orchestration (MoA, LLM-Debate, MAV), which helps frontier LLMs, actually hurts SLMs, and supports this claim with a failure-mode (groupthink) analysis and a prompt-sensitivity study ruling out suboptimal prompting as the cause.

SLM-MUX is simple, training-free, and effective: consistent gains over discussion-based baselines and the best single model across MATH, GPQA, and GSM8K, and the two-SLM ensemble matches or beats Qwen-2.5-72B on GPQA/GSM8K.

Good breadth of validation: model-selection search with union-accuracy/contradiction objectives, compute-scaling analyses in two dimensions, test-set verification of scaling trends, search-set stability analysis, a random-selection baseline isolating architecture vs. search contributions, and generalization experiments on HumanEval, frontier LLMs, and domain-specific fine-tuned models.

The paper is honest about limitations (static model selection, non-adaptive tie-breaking, weakness of self-consistency as a confidence signal) and includes theoretical support (Hoeffding-style bound) plus a comparative analysis explaining why per-question routing beats pooled voting.
Reasonably reproducible: experimental settings, temperatures, sample counts, validation-set construction, and dataset licenses are documented, and baselines use original code/prompts.
weaknesses: Limited novelty of the core mechanism: SLM-MUX essentially performs per-question routing to the model with the highest self-consistency score, with validation-accuracy tie-breaking. Confidence/consistency-based selection is well established in prior work (some of which the authors cite, e.g., Taubenfeld et al. 2025), so the main methodological contribution is an application/adaptation rather than a new technique.

The headline comparison against the strongest simple baseline is not fully supported: in Table 1, Single-Best-SC achieves 42.4 ± 3.5 on GPQA vs. SLM-MUX's 42.1 ± 0.3, so SLM-MUX does not beat self-consistency on that benchmark, yet the abstract claims broad superiority. Gains over SC are modest and sometimes within noise.

Compute-fairness concerns: SLM-MUX uses multiple models and multiple samples per model, so it consumes substantially more inference compute than Single-Best or Single-Best-SC. The comparison to Qwen-2.5-72B in Table 4 does not report the total token/energy budget of the two-SLM ensemble versus the 72B model, weakening the 'small models rival a large model' narrative.

The theoretical analysis rests on an idealized assumption that incorrect answers are scattered rather than clustered; in practice SLMs frequently share the same wrong answer (which is exactly why the contradiction penalty is needed), and the bound does not cover confidently-wrong models, the method's known failure mode.

Scope is narrow: primarily multiple-choice/exact-answer math and QA benchmarks, with only a preliminary open-ended extension using an ad-hoc embedding-based consistency estimator whose correlation with correctness is asserted but not deeply analyzed.

The exhaustive-search model selection uses a 500-question validation set and λ=1 without sensitivity analysis of λ, and Table 2's 'Group 2' combinations include dominated pairs (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B + Llama3.1-8B, where one dominates the other per Figure 4's own logic), which the paper does not reconcile.
